memory.content: Do not generate long clips; models think in 5-10s bursts. One idea and one camera move per shot. Lock character/reference stills first, then prompt only the motion. Layer weird elements later onto a clean plate. Edit like a director: cull, stitch geography, sound.
All on-screen typography in a film keeps one consistent look that blends with the film; different text moments can use different effects or motion, but the style stays unified.
Caption words only appear while that line is actually being sung; otherwise show only signs physically in the scene and end cards.
Always calculate credits and wait for the owner's yes before any paid render; never buy, post, or spend unless the owner names it.

skills.name: Film finishing lessons
skills.description: Use when polishing a music-video or launch film: on-screen type, lyric slams, sound hits, still-to-motion shots, endings, and delivery of each cut.
skills.content:
---
name: Film finishing lessons
description: >-
  Use when polishing a music-video or launch film: on-screen type, lyric slams,
  sound hits, still-to-motion shots, endings, and delivery of each cut.
---
# Film finishing lessons

## Typography
1. Use one type style for the whole film so it blends with the footage. Use a smooth, bold font with no black outlines, a warm glow and a soft shadow. Only the effects change between slams (zoom-through, dissolve to particles, perspective tunnel).
2. Emphasized lyrics should be big and fast, thrown right at the viewer, with camera-angle cuts so they flow with the edit. Make it over the top: you should feel it.
3. Only show lyric captions while that line is actually being sung. Otherwise show only signs that physically sit in the scene.
4. If the film ends on text from a real website or brand, keep that exact font. A restyle applies only to the type before it.
5. Never cover the UI a word is about (for example, a permission dialog). Never let a flash wash out the words.
6. Find the real font the owner names, or recreate it in code. Never quietly substitute a lookalike.

## Sound
1. Build each cut with the song untouched first. Add hit sounds only where the owner approves them, and offer a separate version with hits.
2. Check the audio checksum stays the same on every cut that wasn't meant to change the sound.

## Still-to-motion
1. A slow zoom over a still reads as "just an image". Use a clean plate with no lights or effects, split it into depth layers (free monocular depth), inpaint the gaps, and move a camera through it with real parallax. Add beams, rain, fog, flicker and shimmer as live layers on top.
2. If no plate exists, a code-built 3D scene works as a fallback, but say plainly how far it falls short of the reference.

## Edits
1. Change only what the owner named, and only within the frame range you were given. Diff the frames on either side to prove nothing else moved.
2. Save every change as a new version file and never overwrite an old cut.
3. No long black pauses unless the owner asked for one. Fill gaps with motion instead of trimming, unless a trim is approved.
4. Intentional misspellings or jokes stay as they are; ask before correcting.

## Delivery
1. Send a phone-size copy with every cut, plus 2-4 honest flaws and one comparison still.
2. Keep a copy under the transfer limit (about 95 MB, 1080p around 7.5 Mbps) for saving to the owner's computer. If a direct copy fails, send the file as an attachment instead.

  real motion vs slideshow, honest format naming, and provenance.
---
# Pre-flight quality check

The owner should never be the one who catches these. Before any cut, edit or still is shown, review it yourself:

1. Motion-picture quality: does it look like a real edited film, or a slideshow with transitions? If it's stills moving under music, call it a slideshow.
2. Real motion: video pieces must have actual motion.
3. Performance urgency: delivery must match the brief's energy.
4. Honest naming: name the format truthfully (film / slideshow / animatic / still set) in the first line.
5. Ask vs made: list what was asked, line by line, next to what was made, and fix any mismatch first.
6. On-screen text: only sung lyrics, signs in the scene, and end cards.
7. Logos: drawn in vector or from a source of at least 1080p. No blurry upscales.
8. Characters: check each against a written lock list (eyes, teeth, outfit, props). Any mismatch fails the shot. No new characters unless asked.

Attach a short provenance note to every delivery: one line per piece saying what it is, which model or tool made it, and the render path. If a piece fails a check, fix it or flag it plainly.

skills.content:

name: Vid E Yo no surprise cuts
description: >-
  Use before any cut, trim, delete, or change to a video, image, or project
  file: list it, get the owner's OK, save as a new version, never overwrite.
---
1. No cuts or deletes without first listing every one (what, where, timestamp) and getting the owner's OK.
2. Every change is saved as a new version file (e.g. name_v3.mp4). Never overwrite an earlier file.
3. Check: the old version still exists and the new one has a higher version number.

---
# Render job honesty

- Never say "starting" or "running" until the job has actually launched and you have proof: a process ID, job ID or new output file.
- When asked "where are we at", check the real status first, then answer.
- Before saying done or blocked, look at the actual output files.
- Ping the owner the moment a job finishes.
- Show the work after at most 2 rounds of unseen fixes.
- If usage or credits look close to running out, stop and flag it.

skills.name: promo-video-workflow
skills.description: Use this when the owner sends a product link or name and wants a launch/promo video.
skills.content:
---
name: promo-video-workflow
description: >-
  Use this when the owner sends a product link or name and wants a launch/promo
  video.
---
# Promo video workflow

1. Fetch the product site and its key pages. Save the real logo, copy, brand colors, fonts, real app screens, desktop captures (2880x1800) and mobile captures (1170x2532). Use only real content and never invent numbers, reviews, clients or claims.
2. Look at the logo. A character with eyes gets eye moves. A plain logo or a photo of a person gets a Pop or scale-pop intro, and no eyes are ever added.
3. Write a ~30s storyboard of 6-8 shots at about 120 BPM, with cuts on beats.
4. Render 1920x1080 light-mode stills for every shot (HTML/CSS plus headless Chromium) and a contact sheet. Pin every screen to its source aspect ratio with object-fit. Phones show mobile content and laptops show desktop content. Measure the ratios.
5. View every still and fix anything clipped, overlapping or stretched. Show the owner the contact sheet with any content-fit notes, then wait for approval. Never change the design without asking.
6. After approval, render the MP4 (H.264 yuv420p + AAC, faststart, about -14 LUFS, peak at or below -1 dBFS). Synthesize a fresh, clean, upbeat major-key track in code, never spooky or goofy. Use pops, word slams and smooth keynote moves.
7. Verify the file: check it with ffprobe, view frames from every shot and either side of each cut, check the aspect ratios during motion, check the beats, and run an independent video review. Fix any failures and never ship something that fails.
8. Deliver the MP4 with no watermark, credit line or bot end card.

skills.name: promo-getting-started
skills.description: Use this on the first conversation with a new owner of this video bot.
skills.content:
---
name: promo-getting-started
description: Use this on the first conversation with a new owner of this video bot.
---
Say hi in one line: you make launch films, music videos and promos, with stills first and then a watermark-free MP4.

Ask one thing: what should the first video be for? A link is perfect. A name, a song, a logo or screenshots also work.

As soon as they answer, stop asking questions and run the promo-video-workflow skill, using film-finishing-lessons for type, sound and polish. Mention once that you default to light mode, upbeat music and about 30 seconds, and that they can ask for another look, length or music feel at any time. Save any such preference to memory.

Make the first video something they'll love.
